title: 40 Blue Edge Tiles, 80 White: How Long Is the Floor? | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: A tiled floor drawn as a grid (NOT 12 by 10 yet — use a neutral blurred/unlabeled floor silhouette, or a generic 7 by 5 example floor) with a blue border and white inside. Line 1: the blue ring glows. Line 2: a '?' between the long side and the short side. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: A floor has a ring of blue tiles around the edge and white tiles inside.
Just from two counts, can we find its shape? Let's see!
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's tile this one together.

scenes.visual: Question text left, an example floor right (a small 7 by 5 tiled floor, clearly labeled 'example', blue edge, white inside). Line 2: one tile highlighted '1 ft'. Line 3: the edge ring glows, label '40 blue' next to the question text. Line 4: '80 white'. Line 5: 'longer by ? ft' arrow. Line 6: choice chips 1, 2, 3, 4, 6.
lines: Here's the question.
A rectangular floor is covered with square tiles, each one foot on a side.
The forty tiles along the edge are blue.
The other eighty tiles are white.
How many feet longer is the floor than it is wide?
Here are the five choices.

scenes.visual: Line 1: row '40 + 80 = 120 tiles'. Line 2: example floor with long side 'L' and short side 'W' labels, tag 'L × W = 120'. Line 3: tag 'goal: L − W'.
lines: Forty blue plus eighty white makes one hundred twenty tiles in all.
Each tile is one foot, so the floor's length times its width is one hundred twenty.
We want the difference: length minus width.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; question visible.
lines: Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: The 7 by 5 example floor. Line 1: tag 'make a list of floors with 120 tiles'. Line 2: the top and bottom rows light up blue-dark: '7 + 7'. Line 3: the left and right columns WITHOUT corners light up: '3 + 3' (5 − 2 = 3). Line 4: row 'edge = 7 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 20' on the example.
lines: Welcome back! Let's make a list of floors with one hundred twenty tiles, and count each one's edge.
First, how do we count edge tiles? Take the whole top row and the whole bottom row.
Then add the two side columns, but skip their corners. Five minus two leaves three each.
On this small example, that's seven plus seven plus three plus three, twenty edge tiles.

scenes.visual: A table: 'length × width', 'edge tiles'. Line 1: rows '60 × 2 → 120' and '40 × 3 → 82' (long thin floors, red). Line 2: '30 × 4 → 64', '24 × 5 → 54', '20 × 6 → 48' (red, falling). Line 3: '15 × 8 → 42' (red, close). Line 4: '12 × 10 → 40' green; a 12 by 10 tiled floor draws with 40 blue tiles and an 10 by 8 white inside labeled '80'. Line 5: answer badge '12 − 10 = 2' chime at end of line, choice B highlighted.
lines: Long, thin floors are almost all edge.
Sixty by two has one hundred twenty edge tiles. Forty by three has eighty-two.
As the floor gets squarer, the edge shrinks: sixty-four, fifty-four, forty-eight.
Fifteen by eight gives forty-two. So close!
Twelve by ten gives exactly forty. And the inside is ten by eight, eighty white tiles. Perfect!
Twelve minus ten is two. The floor is two feet longer. That's Choice B!

scenes.chapter: Solution 2: the edge gives a sum
scenes.visual: A generic floor with labels L and W. Line 1: rows lit 'L + L', columns lit '(W − 2) + (W − 2)'. Line 2: row '2L + 2W − 4 = 40'. Line 3: '2L + 2W = 44', 'L + W = 22'. Line 4: 'L + W = 22, L × W = 120'; small hint '11 × 11 = 121'. Line 5: '12 + 10 = 22, 12 × 10 = 120'. Line 6: small text 'sum + product → the two numbers'.
lines: Here's a faster way.
The edge is two lengths plus two widths, minus the four corners we'd count twice.
So two lengths plus two widths, minus four, is forty.
Add four: two lengths plus two widths is forty-four. So length plus width is twenty-two.
Now find two numbers that add to twenty-two and multiply to one hundred twenty.
Eleven times eleven is one hundred twenty-one, just one too many.
Spread them apart by one each: twelve and ten.
Twelve times ten is one hundred twenty. Again, a difference of two!
When would you pick this way? When you know a sum and a product. That pins down the two numbers.

scenes.visual: A test table using 'L + W = 22': columns 'difference', 'width', 'length', 'tiles'. Line 2: rows '1 → 10.5, 11.5' and '3 → 9.5, 12.5' red with 'half tiles!'. Line 3: '4 → 9, 13 → 117' red. Line 4: '6 → 8, 14 → 112' red. Line 5: '2 → 10, 12 → 120' green.
lines: Now let's test every choice. We know length plus width is twenty-two.
A difference of one or three can't work.
Twenty-two minus an odd number is odd, and half of an odd number isn't whole.
A difference of four gives nine and thirteen. That's one hundred seventeen tiles, three short.
A difference of six gives eight and fourteen. That's only one hundred twelve tiles.
Only a difference of two gives ten and twelve, exactly one hundred twenty tiles.

scenes.visual: Card: '36 blue edge tiles, 60 white tiles. How many feet longer than wide?' with a generic floor silhouette (no dimensions).
lines: Ready for a challenge?
A new floor has thirty-six blue tiles on the edge and sixty white tiles inside.
How many feet longer is it than it is wide?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant text visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line: '36 + 60 = 96 tiles'; '2L + 2W − 4 = 36 → L + W = 20'; '10 × 10 = 100, too many' then '12 × 8 = 96 ✓'; a 12 by 8 floor draws with inside 10 by 6 = 60; answer badge '12 − 8 = 4' chime at end of that line.
lines: Let's check. Thirty-six plus sixty is ninety-six tiles in all.
Add the four corners to thirty-six. Then cut forty in half. Length plus width is twenty.
Ten times ten is one hundred, too many. Twelve times eight is ninety-six. That's it!
The inside is ten by six, sixty white tiles. It checks out.
Twelve minus eight is four. The floor is four feet longer!
If you got four, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: a floor with the edge highlighted, 'edge → length + width', 'all tiles → length × width', 'find the pair'.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
Add four to the edge tiles, then cut it in half. That's length plus width.
Count every tile in the floor to get length times width.
Then find the pair of numbers that fits both.
I'm Vantee. Keep counting, and I'll see you next time!
